1.title: CONTINUOUS & DISPERSED PHASE
1.question: In a mayonnaise system, which statement correctly identifies the continuous and dispersed phases?

options.text: Oil = continuous phase, water = dispersed phase
Water = continuous phase, oil = dispersed phase
Gas = continuous phase, oil = dispersed phase
Solid = continuous phase, water = dispersed phase

1.hint: Mayonnaise is an oil-in-water (O/W) emulsion. Think about which phase surrounds the droplets.
1.explanation: Mayonnaise is an oil-in-water (O/W) emulsion. Water forms the continuous phase that surrounds dispersed oil droplets. Lecithin from egg yolk acts as the emulsifier, adsorbing at the oil–water interface to stabilise the system and prevent coalescence.

2.title: EMULSIFIER MECHANISM
2.question: How does lecithin stabilise an emulsion?

options.text: Reduces surface tension between oil and water

2.hint: Lecithin is amphiphilic — it has a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail. Think about where it sits and what that does to the interface.
2.explanation: Lecithin is an amphiphilic molecule: its hydrophilic phosphate head group orients toward water and its hydrophobic fatty acid tails orient toward oil. This adsorption at the oil–water interface reduces interfacial tension, lowering the energy cost of creating and maintaining small droplets and forming a physical barrier that prevents coalescence.

3.title: EMULSION TYPE
3.question: Milk is best classified as which type of emulsion?
3.hint: Milk is predominantly water (~87%). The fat is the minor phase — think about which phase is dispersed and which is continuous.
3.explanation: Milk is an oil-in-water (O/W) emulsion: fat globules (dispersed phase, ~3.5–5% fat) are suspended in an aqueous continuous phase (~87% water). Milk proteins, particularly casein micelles and whey proteins, adsorb at the fat globule membrane and provide electrostatic and steric stabilisation against coalescence.

4.title: EMULSION FORMATION
4.question: Arrange the three stages of emulsion formation in the correct order:
4.hint: First the two phases must be brought together, then mechanical energy breaks droplets apart, then they are stabilised.
4.explanation: Emulsion formation proceeds in 3 stages: (1) Dispersion — the two immiscible phases are brought together, (2) Droplet disruption — mechanical energy (homogenisation, shear) breaks the dispersed phase into fine droplets, (3) Stabilisation — emulsifiers adsorb at the interface and form a protective film to prevent coalescence.

5.title: FACTORS AFFECTING EMULSION
5.question: Which factor is NOT directly important in emulsion formation and stability?
5.hint: Three of these factors alter the physical or chemical environment during emulsification. The fourth is purely an aesthetic attribute.
5.explanation: Temperature affects viscosity, interfacial tension, and emulsifier adsorption rate. Energy input (homogenisation, ultrasound) determines droplet size. Phase ratio determines the volume fraction of dispersed phase and influences stability limits (e.g. phase inversion). Colour is an aesthetic property with no effect on the physicochemical processes governing emulsion formation or stability.

6.title: DROPLET SIZE & STABILITY
6.question: In an emulsion, smaller droplet size generally leads to:
6.hint: Recall Stokes' Law — the rate of creaming or sedimentation depends on the square of the droplet radius.
6.explanation: According to Stokes' Law, the creaming/sedimentation velocity is proportional to r² (droplet radius squared). Smaller droplets therefore rise or settle far more slowly, giving better kinetic stability. Smaller droplets also present a greater surface area-to-volume ratio, allowing more emulsifier coverage per unit volume, further resisting coalescence and Ostwald ripening.

7.title: EMULSION INSTABILITY
7.question: Match each emulsion instability mechanism to its correct description:

rightItems.text: Droplets rise due to density difference
Growth of large droplets at expense of small ones

7.hint: Creaming = gravity; Flocculation = loose clusters (reversible); Coalescence = permanent fusion; Ostwald = solubility gradient; Phase inversion = O/W becomes W/O; Breaking = total collapse.
7.explanation: Six instability mechanisms: Creaming — droplets rise (or sediment) due to density difference with continuous phase; Flocculation — droplets aggregate loosely but remain intact (reversible); Coalescence — droplets merge permanently reducing interfacial area; Ostwald ripening — molecules migrate from small to large droplets via continuous phase; Phase inversion — O/W switches to W/O or vice versa; Breaking — complete irreversible separation of oil and water.

8.title: GEL STRUCTURE
8.question: In a gel system, which phase forms the continuous network?
8.hint: A gel behaves like a solid because of a continuous 3D framework — not because of the liquid it traps.
8.explanation: In a gel, the solid polymer network (crosslinked biopolymer chains) forms the continuous phase that gives the gel its solid-like mechanical properties. The liquid (water or solvent) is immobilised within this network. This is why gels exhibit viscoelastic behaviour — they resist deformation like a solid yet show some flow characteristics.

9.title: GEL TYPE
9.question: Which description best characterises a homogeneous gel?

options.text: Gas bubbles trapped in solid matrix

9.hint: Homogeneous means consistent and uniform at the molecular level — no visible regions of different composition.
9.explanation: A homogeneous gel features a uniform molecular network in which biopolymer chains are crosslinked or entangled evenly throughout the continuous phase, with no visible phase separation. Examples include gelatin gels and agar gels. Heterogeneous gels, by contrast, have regions of varying polymer concentration or phase composition visible at the micro- or macroscale.

10.title: GEL NETWORK FORMATION
10.question: Match each gel network mechanism to its correct description:
10.hint: Ionic crosslinking needs divalent cations (e.g. Ca²⁺). Hydrophobic = non-polar regions avoiding water.
10.explanation: Gel networks form via four mechanisms: Hydrogen bonding — polar –OH and –NH groups attract through water bridges (e.g. gelatin, starch); Ionic crosslinking — divalent cations like Ca²⁺ bridge negatively charged polymer chains (e.g. alginate gelation); Hydrophobic interaction — non-polar segments minimise contact with water by clustering together (e.g. casein micelles); Chain entanglement — long polymer chains become physically interlocked at sufficient concentration.

11.title: GEL FORMATION FACTORS
11.question: Which factor does NOT directly influence gelation?
11.hint: Three of these factors alter the physical environment of the polymer chains — the fourth is only an aesthetic property.
11.explanation: pH affects the ionisation of functional groups on biopolymers, altering charge and crosslinking potential. Ionic strength screens electrostatic repulsion, allowing closer chain–chain interaction. Sugar competes for water, reducing water activity and promoting network formation. Colour intensity is an aesthetic attribute with no effect on the molecular interactions driving gelation.

12.title: FOAM PHASES
12.question: Whipped cream is best classified as which type of colloidal system?
12.hint: Whipped cream is still pourable/spreadable — its matrix has not set solid. The bubbles are the dispersed phase.
12.explanation: Whipped cream is a gas-in-liquid foam: air bubbles (dispersed phase) are incorporated into liquid cream (continuous phase). Partially crystallised fat globules and adsorbed milk proteins stabilise the air–liquid interface. The foam remains fluid enough to spread yet holds its aerated structure temporarily.

13.title: FOAM CLASSIFICATION
13.question: Bread is an example of which colloidal foam type?
13.hint: Baking sets the bread structure — what was liquid during proving becomes solid in the oven.
13.explanation: Bread is a gas-in-solid foam. During proving, yeast fermentation produces CO₂ gas bubbles dispersed in the liquid dough. Baking gelatinises starch and denatures gluten proteins, setting a solid continuous matrix around the gas cells. The result is a permanent solid foam with characteristic porous crumb structure.

14.title: FOAM FORMATION
14.question: Arrange the three stages of food foam formation in the correct order:
14.hint: Air must enter first, then molecules rush to the interface, then a lasting film develops.
14.explanation: Foam formation occurs in 3 stages: (1) Bubble incorporation — air or gas is introduced into the liquid phase by mechanical agitation (whipping, beating), (2) Surface stabilisation — amphiphilic molecules (proteins, surfactants) rapidly adsorb at the air–liquid interface, lowering surface tension, (3) Film formation — a coherent, elastic interfacial film develops between adjacent bubbles, resisting drainage and coalescence to maintain foam structure.

15.title: FOAM STABILITY FACTORS
15.question: Which factor improves food foam stability?

options.text: Weak protein film at the interface

15.hint: Foam collapses when the thin film between bubbles drains or ruptures — what prevents that?
15.explanation: A strong, elastic interfacial protein layer is the primary stabilising factor in food foams. Denatured proteins (e.g. egg white albumin) unfold and cross-link at the air–water interface, forming a viscoelastic film that resists drainage, bubble coalescence, and disproportionation. Low continuous-phase viscosity accelerates drainage; a weak protein film offers little mechanical resistance; high temperature typically destabilises foams by reducing surface viscosity and accelerating drainage.

16.title: COLLOID TYPES
16.question: Which of the following is NOT classified as a colloidal system?
16.hint: Colloids contain dispersed particles in the 1–1000 nm range. A dissolved crystal creates ions far smaller than this.
16.explanation: Sols, emulsions, and foams are all colloidal dispersions with dispersed particles or droplets in the 1–1000 nm size range. A crystalline salt solution is a true molecular solution — the ions (e.g. Na⁺, Cl⁻) are dissolved at sub-nanometre scale and are not colloidal particles. It therefore falls outside the colloidal classification.

17.title: COLLOID CLASSIFICATION
17.question: Hydrophilic colloids are best described as:
17.hint: Break the word down — 'hydro' means water, 'philic' means loving. What does that tell you about their interaction with water?
17.explanation: Hydrophilic colloids (literally 'water-loving') are colloidal systems whose dispersed phase has a strong affinity for water. Biopolymers such as proteins and polysaccharides form hydrophilic colloids because their polar and charged groups interact favourably with water molecules, keeping them dispersed. These systems are generally more stable than hydrophobic colloids because the water–particle interaction reduces the tendency for aggregation.

18.title: THERMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY
18.question: Which instability mechanism involves thermodynamically driven growth of large particles at the expense of small ones? Type the name of the mechanism.
18.hint: This process is named after a Nobel laureate and is driven by the Kelvin effect — small particles have higher chemical potential than large ones.
18.explanation: Ostwald ripening is a thermodynamically driven process based on the Kelvin (Gibbs–Thomson) effect: smaller droplets/particles have a higher chemical potential than larger ones due to their greater curvature. Molecules diffuse through the continuous phase from small to large particles, causing small ones to shrink and disappear while large ones grow, progressively coarsening the dispersion.

19.title: HYDROCOLLOID SELECTION
19.question: Which factor is MOST important when selecting a hydrocolloid for a food application?

options.text: pH stability and ionic strength compatibility
Packaging type used for the product

19.hint: Hydrocolloids are polyelectrolytes — their functional behaviour changes dramatically with the charge environment of the food.
19.explanation: pH and ionic strength are the primary functional determinants for hydrocolloids. pH affects the ionisation of carboxyl and amino groups, directly altering solubility, gelation temperature, and network strength. Ionic strength screens electrostatic interactions between polymer chains. Colour, taste preference, and packaging are extrinsic factors unrelated to hydrocolloid functional performance in a food matrix.

20.title: NON-NEWTONIAN RHEOLOGY
20.question: Most food emulsions and sauces display shear-thinning (pseudoplastic) behavior. How does viscosity change as shear rate increases?

options.text: Viscosity remains completely constant regardless of shear rate
Viscosity decreases as shear rate increases due to structural alignment
Viscosity increases continuously as shear rate increases

20.hint: Think about how shaking or stirring salad dressing makes it pour easily.
20.explanation: Shear-thinning fluids experience a decrease in apparent viscosity at higher shear rates because entangled polymers or droplet clusters align in the direction of flow.

21.title: PHASE INVERSION TEMPERATURE
21.question: What occurs when a non-ionic surfactant-stabilised O/W emulsion is heated above its Phase Inversion Temperature (PIT)?

options.text: The surfactant becomes more hydrophilic and forms a rigid gel
Dehydration makes the surfactant lipophilic, causing inversion to a W/O emulsion
The water phase boils away leaving dry oil
Droplets shrink to nanometer scale automatically

21.hint: Heating dehydrates polyoxyethylene chains, altering surfactant preferred curvature.
21.explanation: At the PIT, non-ionic surfactants dehydrate and become lipophilic, driving preferred interfacial curvature to flip the emulsion from O/W to W/O.

22.title: THIXOTROPIC BEHAVIOUR
22.question: Ketchup and hydrocolloid sauces exhibit thixotropy. How do thixotropic fluids behave under constant shear over time?

options.text: Viscosity decreases over time under shear and gradually recovers at rest
Viscosity increases indefinitely over time under shear
Viscosity fluctuates randomly irrespective of time
The fluid turns into a permanent elastic crystalline solid

22.hint: Thixotropy is time-dependent structural breakdown and recovery.
22.explanation: Thixotropy is a time-dependent shear-thinning phenomenon where continuous shear breaks down internal physical networks over time, lowering viscosity until structure rebuilds during rest.

config.missionBriefingText:
The Food Colloids Kitchen has suffered a catastrophic system failure. Emulsions are breaking, gels have collapsed, foams have drained, and the master colloid database is corrupted. Your mission: navigate through 4 laboratory rooms, solve food colloid puzzles, and restore stability before the system shuts down permanently.

  • Solve all puzzles per room to unlock the exit code
  • Enter codes correctly to proceed between rooms
  • Complete all 4 rooms to unlock the final clearance
  • Score points for correct answers; hints cost 10 points each

Good luck, Colloid Scientist.
